blocks.raw: <Note>Colonial architecture is not purely Spanish—it is a hybrid creation shaped by indigenous craftspeople, who adapted Spanish Baroque forms to local materials, climate, and pre-existing spatial traditions. This synthesis is called mestizo Baroque.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Do not confuse the plaza mayor with indigenous gathering spaces, though they share a central function. The Laws of the Indies plaza is orthogonal, gridded, and explicitly hierarchical (cathedral + government buildings at fixed positions). Indigenous plazas were pre-contact but adapted into the colonial model—the plaza is syncretic, not purely European.</Warn>

<ExamTip>**Pattern 1: Urban Planning Recognition**
Questions ask you to identify the Laws of the Indies principles in a town plan diagram—orthogonal grid, plaza at center, cathedral dominance, radiating streets. You must name the planning system and explain why Spanish colonizers used it.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 2: Building Function and Form**
Questions present colonial churches or civic buildings and ask why they were designed a certain way—fortress-like walls (defense), thick masonry (climate control), multiple chapels (conversion of indigenous populations). You connect form to colonial function.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw:
<ExamTip>**Pattern 3: Regional Variation**
Questions distinguish colonial architecture across regions: Mexican Baroque differs from Peruvian mestizo style differs from Caribbean island adaptations. You recognize local materials and indigenous influence while identifying shared Spanish colonial principles.</ExamTip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Treating plaza mayor as purely European. The plaza is not a straight Spanish import. Indigenous communities had central gathering spaces; colonizers adapted this tradition into the Laws of the Indies orthogonal model. Colonial architecture is fusion, not replacement.", "Ignoring defensive architecture. Many colonial churches are fortress-like because they were fortresses. Students overlook gun ports, minimal windows, and thick walls as defensive features. A church with a gun port is not a design accident—it reflects 16th-century colonial military reality."]} />
